Fighting yesterday’s enemy, who no longer exists, so that one does not have to face the real and present enemy of today. This is the ugliest form of continuing the war.
At the same time, it is the most contemptible form of cowardly evasion and the most dishonest form of pacifism.
Keep kicking at the crimes of the defeated, armed with all the licenses granted by the current victor.
The victor secures immunity for his own crimes by appointing himself judge over the crimes of the defeated.
Eventually they will make Christ himself an O. d. F.—a “Victim of Fascism”—and tolerate his cult on that basis.
How touchingly static and mechanical this is:
The point is no longer to lever the world off its hinges, but to “change” it—that is, to infect it.
The poû stō, the place on which to stand, is nothingness.
Read several notes from the spring of 1933.
An electron-world of numinous meanings and feelings.
A Milky Way of symbolically glittering concepts.
To Heinrich Weinstock, with a copy of my lecture of February 1941:
The introduction to Thucydides is in fact a Historiographeia in nuce—a theory of historical writing in miniature.
(Remember my note on Tocqueville, and Hobbes’s introduction to his translation of Thucydides.)
Hobbes, with his overpowering objectivity, belongs to that glorious chorus.
(To Wilhelm Grewe, concerning the discussion of Nuremberg as a legal question and his accompanying letter:)

I have read your remarks with the greatest care and have come to the conviction that something infinitely more important becomes visible here, far beyond the expert precision of your argument: namely, that we in Germany still stand at the center of thought, and that we must work through the most terrible problems entirely within ourselves, without any help from West or East, Right or Left.
We are carrying out a trial within ourselves: subjugated, quartered, trampled underfoot, and yet “annihilated in nothing.”

The intellectual achievement and style of your argument show me that neither West nor East can today boast that it knows itself, us, and the present world better than we know that world and ourselves. That is the general impression I received from reading your argument.

Your remarks are, of course, framed within a discussion and therefore contain all the considerations, restrictions, reservations, tactical advantages and disadvantages, and everything else that such framing necessarily brings with it.

You have managed to secure a considerable amount of room for your own line of thought. But in the end the whole thing still appears as a discussion. And it is neither my place nor appropriate for me to take part in it.

I do not count occasional curiosities as participation—for example, the involuntary recollection that the passage from 2 Samuel 12:5 cited by your opponent on p. 73 is used by Hobbes as an example of a tyrannical desire to kill and of a violation of the principle nulla poena sine lege, no punishment without prior law. So I remain outside the discussion.
I therefore want only to indicate two things about what you say.

I consider your question about the Gerichtsherr, the actual authority standing behind the tribunal, on p. 10 to be essential, and I think one can insist upon it even in this introduction. It would be revealing to ask historically, sociologically, and psychologically who the real master—or masters—of this proceeding actually were. That question forced itself visibly enough upon the whole world in the treatment of the Katyn case. It may also touch upon the strange fact that the supposed aggressor liked to imagine that he could still wage a old-style war toward the West, while toward the East he believed he could afford a discriminatory war <…>.
Two fronts also meant <…> two kinds of war.

I consider it a great and decisive methodological achievement that you separate the question of criminalizing aggressive war as such from the question of the other crimes—inhumanities and war crimes—and that you state this distinction consciously, clearly, and forcefully, raising it to the level of a basic principle on p. 99.
Without that distinction there can be no scientific discussion of the trial, either as a whole or in its individual parts.

Nor can there be any legal understanding of an offense as new and difficult as aggressive war, with all the new problems involved in precisely defining the prohibited act, identifying the circle of possible perpetrators, and determining the relation between earlier definitions of “aggression,” which had been conceived in purely terms, and the substantive problem of responsibility for war and the justa causa belli, the just cause of war. And then there is the entire problem of <…> forcing one to jump <…>, which is far too to be thrown out into the street.
The problem of creating new crimes and new penalties must trouble every thoughtful jurist who knows what has already happened in the legal history of civil war.

Beginning with “heresy” and “tyranny”—along with fine related offenses such as flattery and favoritism. Then the modern dissolution of criminal law into the extermination of pests and troublemakers. And finally the biological criminalization of illness in Samuel Butler’s Erewhon, something we hardly dare laugh at anymore after our own experiences.
The victorious Northern states committed horrifying atrocities in 1864. But apparently they neglected to declare the slaveholders retroactive criminal offenders.

In future civil wars, people will probably not make that mistake. That you separate this great problem—the criminalization of aggressive war as such—with complete clarity from other kinds of crime is an important achievement. Given the present situation, doing so requires as much tact as intellectual and moral courage.
I say this to you openly and without hesitation, especially as I remember our mutual friend Wilhelm Ahlmann, although, as I said, I cannot take part in your discussion myself.
So, with thanks, I confirm that I have received what you sent me. With every good wish for you and your work,

On 4 April 1948, while sunk in the most helpless depression, I was suddenly and comfortingly distracted by the discovery of an astonishing phrase. Goethe’s genius for language—which never stops astonishing me—had tossed it off casually, almost in passing, in a letter to Johann H. Meyer dated 6 June 1797. He says that in Wallenstein, when all is said and done, everything depends on the mass of the army itself—yes, the army as a mass—which no longer remains with Wallenstein “as soon as he changes the formula of service.”
I could hardly believe my eyes or ears.

I have never come across anything more exact on the subject of legitimacy and legality, because the phrase captures both things at once: the sheer weight of the mass, and the apparently formal nothingness of a mere formula.

(And incidentally, Goethe is magnificent on the question of exposition: an exposition must not simply communicate the facts. It must be designed to convey the full breadth of an existence and the mood surrounding it.)
There is an orchid that makes itself look ugly, like a blowfly, in order to protect both itself and the honey it produces from actual flies.
Did that do you any good?
What is all this talk supposed to mean?
No one will give up the criminalization of the enemy if it proves to be an effective weapon. But in the hands of the West it is not an effective weapon, and cannot be one.
If the West handles its atomic bombs as amateurishly as it handles this weapon—the criminalization of the aggressor—they will be more likely to fall on its own roof than even to touch the real enemy.
I can read Kasack’s The City Beyond the River only as far as Part II, Chapter XIII, p. 290. Then it suddenly turns into caricature and anti-literature. A pity.
The first part very successfully brings Kubin’s The Other Side and Kafka’s The Trial into the world of 1943–44.
Why do all these gifted writers refuse to listen to Ernst Jünger’s warning against every polemical word?

If polemic is no longer directed immediately and completely against a strong enemy who is fully present and has you directly by the throat—as with Léon Bloy or the young Theodor Haecker—but instead against a dead enemy, it immediately begins to squint sideways and is poisoned by the corpse-toxin of the dead enemy.
Later, when I have recovered from the shock of my disappointment, I will continue reading. I hope I will then also be able to judge the appearance of Wilhelm Ahlmann properly.
Léon Bloy’s influence on Ernst Jünger is an extraordinary problem.
Jünger could approach Bloy, the “pariah,” with his savage hatred of Protestants, Prussians, and Germans only by overcoming the strongest possible revulsion.
But Bloy’s diaries are also a prototype for the whole form of the “diary.” I could even say that they helped create the form.

With one stroke they leave behind all that Romantic and impressionistic rummaging through the soul. They make it impossible to confuse “radiations” with “reflections,” and they give the aphorism a concrete situation instead of letting it flutter away into emptiness.
What is magnificent for me—unexpectedly so, beyond anything one could have calculated—is that Ernst Jünger can appear, in this respect, as Léon Bloy’s heir.
Theodor Haecker had long since lost his strong claim to that great inheritance.

But the profiteurs de Léon Bloy—the people who profited from Bloy—such as Claudel, or still more Maritain, threw the inheritance into the street. In return they received the miserable sinner’s wages of satisfying their hatred of a Germany that had already been trampled underfoot.
The baseness of that hatred makes both of them ripe for the curse of today’s pèlerin de l’Absolu—the pilgrim of the Absolute.
To H. Barion, referring to W. Grewe and the discussion of Nuremberg as a legal question:
I ask him to read it,
“so that you will understand why it matters to me that my memorandum on the criminalization of aggressive war was already complete in the summer of 1945, before the indictment was brought.

It stands as a record of the considerations that any lawyer with the necessary expertise could and should already have made at that time—and which one discriminated German lawyer actually did make, without concealing them from anyone, not even from the CIC [Civil Internment Camp].”
For the sake of the German name, and for every lawyer anywhere in the world who thinks scientifically. Also for the honour of the legal profession itself.
Defamed, discriminated against, dismantled, contaminated, underprivileged on every side.
In a dream I say to the Englishman:
Ripe for the final coup de grâce, like Tsar Nicholas of Russia.

Your last move was to accept the unconditional surrender in Schleswig-Holstein, although you had no right to do so. You did not bring about that surrender. The Russians and Americans did. It was not you, but the Russians and Americans, who were masters of both the conflict and what was at stake in it.
The whole argument becomes murky when I think of H. S. Chamberlain.
Wonderful, the Shakespeare passage Günther Krauss copied into his diary Captivitas:
“It is enough for us to know that we are the king’s subjects. If his cause is wrong, our obedience to the king clears us of the crime.”
“Here lies” is the final part of his story. —Daniel Defoe.
Where do those people lie whose ashes an uncomprehending hunger for revenge scattered across the whole world, in the most un-Christian ignorance of the song:
The ashes will not rest, they scatter through every land?
Could they, through the stupidity of their enemies, have escaped the grave?
Defeated in the name of Christianity, we ask ourselves where this Christianity is actually to be found.

I respect the fact that there is a general fear of a contagion de l’infortune—a contagion of misfortune. That respect even gives me a kind of belated satisfaction in my present status, and allows me to draw something useful from my existence as a peripsēma—an outcast, something cast away.
I say satisfaction in my status, because I can no longer claim the honour that once belonged to that status.
On your question about when the idea of “vested rights” was born:
Taken as a whole, the end of vested rights naturally begins when law is transformed into positivist legality.
